1:
Solomon's own house took thirteen years, and the chapter says so before it says anything else about it. Gill sets that figure beside the seven years the temple had taken and reads the difference as deliberate: the king made more haste with the house of God than with his own, which showed a greater regard to the honour of God than to his own glory, or even to his own convenience. Gill adds that the palace was not begun until the sanctuary was done, so the order of the work is itself part of what is being reported here.

Henry presses the same comparison into a principle. Never had any man so much of the spirit of building as Solomon, he says, nor to better purpose, because the king began with the temple; having built for God first, all his other buildings were comfortable afterwards. Henry will not read the thirteen years as either carelessness or superior care. Solomon was not more exact upon his own house, only less eager and intent upon it — in no haste for a palace, impatient until the sanctuary was finished and fit for use. The lesson Henry draws is plain: we ought to prefer God's honour before our own ease and satisfaction, and the surest foundations of lasting prosperity are those laid in early piety.

Henry also refuses to let the verse become a reproach against David. Solomon's father had built a good house, and it was no reflection upon him that his son built a better, in proportion to the estate with which God had blessed him. Much of the comfort of this life, Henry observes, is bound up with having an agreeable house to live in. The palace is not handled as a vanity needing excuse, but as a good thing taken in its proper order, after the greater one.

Clarke is occupied with where the building stood. He takes it to have been in Jerusalem itself, and suggests it served as the king's winter residence, noting that a later chapter refers to it simply as the king's house. Clarke keeps it distinct from the other great structure described further down, which drew its name from Lebanon. The dwelling in view here is the one Solomon actually lived in, and the thirteen years belong to that.
2:
The second building of the chapter is named for Lebanon, and the witnesses begin by denying that it stood there. Gill points out that Lebanon lay on the northern border of the land, far from Jerusalem, while this house served as both a magazine of arms and a court of judicature — neither of which could be kept at such a distance from the capital. The name came instead from its materials and its setting: built of the cedars of Lebanon, and placed among groves of trees that resembled that country. Gill takes it for a summer house, and notes that the Targum calls it a royal house of refreshment. Clarke likewise denies it was built in Lebanon and thinks it stood on Mount Zion; why the name attached to it he cannot say, though he guesses it was because the materials came almost entirely from there.

Delitzsch offers a different account of the name, and it turns on the architecture rather than on where the timber grew: the house was built, so to speak, of a forest of cedar pillars, and was called after the forest it resembled inside. He records that Arabic usage calls it the house of his arms, since it later served as a keeping-place for weapons, but declines to reduce it to an arsenal; it was probably meant for other purposes as well. The measurements he takes straight from the text — a hundred cubits long, fifty broad, thirty high, resting on four rows of cedar pillars with hewn cedar beams laid over them.

The forty-five pillars, fifteen to a row, divide them. Gill distributes these across the second floor in three rows of fifteen facing east, north and south, carrying beams that formed the floor of the third storey, with a cedar roof above that. Delitzsch argues that the numbers cannot belong to the pillars at all but to the side-chambers, which the lower rows of pillars carried: forty-five rooms in three tiers, each tier a row of fifteen, built one above another rather than side by side, on the pattern of the side buildings of the sanctuary. He says he once read it the other way himself and gave it up, because that left only galleries where the text speaks of chambers.

On the windows the two agree in substance. Gill places them in the second and third storeys on those same three sides, with none to the west, where the porch stood. Delitzsch is drawn instead to a difficulty in the description of the doorways: the text calls them square, and he judges the word fits the openings and outlooks better than the posts and mouldings, since if a doorway were square its frame would be square as a matter of course. He notes a proposed emendation supported by the Greek translators, who rendered the term by a word meaning a broad space. Gill keeps it simple — the doors into the several stories and apartments, their posts and lintels, and the windows above them, were all square. Delitzsch adds that these doorways served both to connect the rooms with one another and to give access to the storeys, reached by stairs that were probably winding.
6:
Three more structures are named in quick succession, and the witnesses spend their effort on how they stood in relation to one another. Gill puts the colonnade at the west end of the house and says no more. Delitzsch gives it fifty cubits by thirty, with a vestibule in front and pillars and a threshold before that, and argues from its place in the list — between the cedar house and the throne room — that it physically stood between them. Because its fifty cubits match the breadth of the cedar house, he takes the whole to have been fifty wide and thirty deep, laid out on the analogy of the sanctuary porch.

Ellicott reaches the same measurement and draws a different conclusion from it. Some authorities make the colonnade an independent structure; the exact agreement of dimensions persuades Ellicott that it was rather an approach to the hall of state, matching that chamber in the arrangement of its columns and perhaps in height too. He reads the closing clause as describing a porch of its own, with pillars and a threshold before them, and takes the threshold for a kind of plinth, or possibly a flight of steps.

On the throne room the difference sharpens. Delitzsch holds that it and the tribunal are one apartment, serving for audience and for justice together, marked off from the colonnade only by the repeated verb of making, and standing immediately beyond it. Ellicott by contrast treats the place of judgment as a distinct building, described only as floored and ceiled with cedar, and reports Fergusson's reconstruction from Assyrian and Persian remains: a square chamber carried on four central columns with the throne between them, open on every side for the public, the king, and his officers. Gill and Clarke are content with its use — Gill recalling the ivory seat from which causes were heard and tried, Clarke noting that one porch was given over to justice, which Solomon administered in person.

The phrase describing the cedar covering, from floor to floor, Delitzsch calls very obscure. He resists the rendering that makes it panelling running up to the roof beams, since the verb ordinarily means to cover rather than to line, and cannot bear one sense here and another a few verses earlier, where it plainly denotes roofing.

Then the dwellings. Gill identifies the king's house as the portion where he actually lived. Delitzsch places it behind the tribunal, its main entrance probably through that chamber — so that Solomon gave judgment and granted audience, quite literally, in the gate of his own palace — and assigns the royal apartments and those of the Egyptian wife a court of their own at the rear of the whole complex. Clarke counts three houses and suspects they formed one building on one site, distinguished by use: the residence, the court-house, and the quarters for the women.
9:
The account turns from plan to material, and the emphasis falls on quality rather than scale. Gill names the costly stones as marble, porphyry and the like, and takes the foundation blocks to be of great price as well as great size. Delitzsch reads the same clause as covering every building so far described, and holds that these stones were dressed to the measure of hewn work and sawn with saws on the inner and the outer face alike — a finish given to what would be seen and to what would not.

The extent of that finish is fixed by two limits, from the foundation up to a term Delitzsch renders as the corbels on which the roof beams rest. He records the alternative honestly: the Greek translators used a word that one scholar took for the battlements guarding a flat roof, which would make the Hebrew term the stone border of the palace roof. Delitzsch refuses it, because the Greek word means the projection of a roof, and more generally any roof-like projection in a building, but never the parapet round a flat roof, which Hebrew names with a different word altogether. The second limit he reads as the outer court, since the text sets this outside over against the great court.

On the masonry itself the two run together. Delitzsch gives the foundation blocks at ten and eight cubits — a length implying corresponding breadth and thickness — with the visible walls above them built of costly stone cut to the measure of hewn work, and cedar. Gill traces the same courses upward: above the foundation, from there to the top of the buildings, the whole walls were of that kind, right up to the ceiling. Neither treats the detail as ornament for its own sake; it is the reason the buildings could be called costly at all.

The great court closes the section, and here Gill is briefest — it surrounded Solomon's house. Delitzsch describes it as formed of three rows of hewn stones and a row of hewn cedar beams, on the pattern of the inner court of the house of the Lord. He defends the comparison grammatically, reading the connecting particle as a mark of likeness and so refusing a proposed emendation as un-Hebraic, and he takes the hall named alongside it to be the pillared hall of the palace rather than the porch of the sanctuary, since its surrounding wall answered to the wall of the hinder court. Ellicott accepts the resemblance to the temple's inner court and draws out what it implies about the whole: an enclosure of three courses of large stones with a cedar coping, evidently taking in the entire palace, and perhaps holding quarters for the guards and the household. There must have been inner courts besides, he says, around which the more public and the more private buildings were grouped.
13:
A second Hiram enters, and every witness begins by separating him from the first. Gill insists this is not the king of Tyre but an artificer living in it, whom Solomon had heard of and whom the king sent over on request; he passes on the name Hyperon, which Clemens of Alexandria gives him. Clarke calls him an intelligent coppersmith of Jewish extraction on his mother's side, probably married into Tyre. Delitzsch notes that the craftsman bore the king's own name, and that the parallel record adds to it a word meaning my father — not a family claim but a title of honour, master or counsellor.

Delitzsch also reads the verb as a pluperfect: Solomon had sent and fetched him, the notice standing here as a supplementary remark rather than as the next event in sequence. Ellicott looks to the Chronicler for the fuller account, where Solomon's first letter asks for a man cunning to work, and the craftsman comes back with the reply.

The parentage is the one point at which the records seem to disagree, and four of the witnesses set themselves to it. This chapter makes his mother a widow of the tribe of Naphtali and his father a Tyrian; the Chronicler calls her one of the daughters of Dan. Delitzsch harmonises briefly — a Danite by birth who married into Naphtali. Gill lays out the options: she may have belonged to the city of Dan, which lay within Naphtali's territory; or her mother may have been the Danite, so that she is called a daughter of Dan while her father was of Naphtali, which is how the Targum and most of the Jewish commentators take it; or she was herself of Dan and her husband of Naphtali. And if there is an error at all, Gill adds, it belongs not to the sacred historian but to the king of Tyre, whose words the Chronicler is reporting. Clarke reaches for much the same solution and is franker about the uncertainty: the king of Tyre may simply have confounded the two tribes, or she was Naphtali by her father and Dan by her mother; the versions and manuscripts offer no help either way.

Henry is not interested in the tribal puzzle but in what the mixture produced. Hiram had the head of a Tyrian and the heart of an Israelite — the ingenuity of the one and the affection of the other toward the house of God — and it was a happy thing that the blood of two nations met in him, since that is precisely what the work required. Ellicott says something close in his own key: the mixed parentage let him enter into the spirit of Israelite worship while bringing the practical skill of his father's city to bear upon it. Henry sets the whole arrangement in a longer line — as the tabernacle had been built with the wealth of Egypt, so the temple was built with the wit of Tyre, and God will serve himself by the common gifts of the children of men. Henry adds one negative observation about the materials: there was no iron about the temple, though David had prepared iron for the things of iron. Delitzsch closes with the text's own verdict, that the man was filled with wisdom and understanding and skill for every work in brass, and came and did all that Solomon gave him.
15:
The pillars are the first things Hiram makes, and the first difficulty is their height. Gill records eighteen cubits apiece here against thirty-five for the pair in the parallel account, which would leave each at seventeen and a half. He offers two ways out: either the round number is used, or half a cubit in each is taken up by the pedestal it stood in, or by the capital it ran up into, so that what the text measures is only what was visible. Clarke converts the figure — some thirty feet — and adds the circumference at twelve cubits, with a founder's admiration: it would be hard even now, he says, to find a workman who could cast masses of that size, whether solid or hollow.

The capitals set on top draw a similar disagreement over numbers. Delitzsch gives five cubits for each, and refuses to reconcile the three cubits reported in a later notice by supposing that they had been cut down over the years; that figure, he judges, rests on a copyist's error, one Hebrew letter standing in for another. Gill is more interested in their shape: the word suggests large ovals in the form of a crown, or, as Ben Gersom took it, two crowns joined together; elsewhere they are called bowls.

For the ornament the witnesses supply different pictures of the same brass. Gill reads the checker work as thick branches of trees with their boughs and leaves curiously wrought, and the chain work as fringes, like those the Jews wore at the skirts of their garments. Delitzsch describes plaited work and twisted cords resembling chains, seven to each capital, and takes the seven for festoons hung round them. Ellicott doubts the number altogether: the reading seven is probably corrupt, and the clause should run that there was a net-work, or lattice-work, for the one capital and a net-work for the other.

The pomegranates follow, and Delitzsch has to repair the text before he can describe them. In the received Hebrew the words for pillars and for pomegranates have been exchanged; some copies preserve the right order, the sense requires it, and so does the comparison with what comes next. Once corrected, the verse gives two rows of pomegranates set round the twisted work to cover the capitals. How the rows stood to the plaiting is not stated, but Delitzsch adopts the usual view: one ran below and one above, so that the festoon of seven cords was enclosed between them. Gill's whole comment on the verse is that the pillars were adorned in this manner — the making named at the start of the sentence is the decorating described at the end of it.
19:
Above the chain-work and its pomegranates the capitals carried a second ornament, and Delitzsch takes the fact as evidence about the first: the plaiting cannot have reached the top, since lily-work crowns it. He describes that upper portion as sculpture in the form of open lilies, set like a crown upon the lower part. Gill reads it the same way — work wrought in the shape of the lily flower opened — and connects it with what stood in the porch. The clause giving four cubits Delitzsch calls obscure, and he resists the proposal that the phrase places the pillars inside the hall, with their capitals taking the weight of the doorway's lintel.

Where they stood is the chapter's sharpest architectural dispute, and Delitzsch settles it from the parallel account, which twice puts them before the house, before the Holy Place. The pillars therefore stood free in front of the hall, one on either side, and not within it holding up the roof; the arguments brought for the other view he finds without force. Gill fixes the spot more narrowly still, against Jarchi: not at the entrance into the temple itself but at the entrance into the porch. Clarke arrives at the same place from another direction — whatever their names promised, the pillars seem to have borne no part of the building, which is why he calls them emblematical.

Ellicott works on the wording. Over against, he says, is better rendered close to; and the belly of the capital means its rounded swell where it comes down to meet the shaft, the junction round which the bands of pomegranate ran. He also finds a plain omission, since the verse should give two hundred in rows round the one capital and two hundred round the other, which is how the total of four hundred is reached elsewhere. Gill cites Lightfoot to much the same effect and reads the sense without the supplement: the capitals stood above the lily-work, which ran out as far as their middle, and the pomegranates filled that band up.

Then the names. Clarke gives them plainly — one meaning he shall establish, the other in strength. Henry doubts they were memorials of the pillar of cloud and fire, as some suppose, and takes them instead for memoranda to the priests and to everyone who came to worship at that door: not to lean on any sufficiency of their own. When the heart wanders in worship, the first name answers it; for the weakness that cannot perform the duty, the second, since it is God who works in us both to will and to do. Henry notes that the pillars bore neither gates nor roof, which is his point — they were there for beauty and for meaning, and the chequer-work, chains, net-work, lilies and rows of pomegranates in bright brass were ordered to please the eye. He reads a second promise in them, that the worship established among that people would stand; and he observes what became of it when the house fell, for the record of the destruction takes particular notice of the breaking of these pillars. Delitzsch, closing, says the repetition of the lily-work in the last verse is explained by how much the emblem carried, and the account of the capitals ends there.
23:
The great basin is called a sea, and Gill explains the name from usage: a large collection of waters went by that word among the Jews, as with the sea of Tiberias. Delitzsch says the same more briefly — it is named for its size — and takes the measurements as a diameter of ten cubits from rim to opposite rim, an external height of five, and a circumference of thirty. He pauses over the proportion: the round numbers come very near the true ratio, which would be more exactly expressed as seven to twenty-two, or a hundred and thirteen to three hundred and fifty-five.

The ornaments beneath the brim are where the two records part. Gill reports them as oval, so that the Targum calls them figures of eggs; elsewhere they are said to resemble oxen, which he takes as heads of oxen with the rest oval, or as gourds bearing such heads and perhaps serving as taps to let the water out. Delitzsch will not have the harmonisation. The word in the parallel text means oxen, not heads of oxen, so it cannot be smoothed that way; it is an error of the pen, one word written for another and then explained by a later hand. The gourds themselves he counts at ten to the cubit in two rows, cast with the vessel rather than added to it, which puts each at a little over two inches across — though how far the rows stood apart he declines to guess.

On the twelve oxen carrying the basin there is no dispute, only different interests. Gill notes they were brass figures of full proportion. Delitzsch works out the arrangement — three facing each quarter of the heavens, their hindquarters turned inward, the sea resting above them — and reckons their height at about five cubits to the back, standing on a metal plate that held them immovable. Henry is struck by the consequence: the basin sat so high that the priests must either have had steps up to it or taps at the bottom to draw from, and the drawers of water for the house of God had the care of keeping it full.

Henry also passes on a suggestion he evidently likes, that the oxen were cast in contempt of the calf Israel had worshipped, so that the people might see there was nothing in such figures worth adoring — fitter, as the writer he quotes puts it, to make posts of than to make gods of. It did not prevent the calves being set up later. What Henry does press is the comparison of scale: the court of the tabernacle had a laver, the court of the temple a sea, and he reads the enlargement as a sign that fuller provision for cleansing came with the gospel than the law had made.

The last details are the metal and the measure. Gill gives the thickness as a handbreadth, four fingers. Delitzsch agrees, matches it to the pillars, and describes the rim as bent outward like the lip of a goblet and worked with lily flowers. On the capacity he again prefers this text to the parallel: two thousand baths, not three, since the dimensions given cannot hold more, and the larger figure comes of confusing two Hebrew letters. The purpose he states plainly — water kept ready for the priests to wash before they came to the altar or entered the Holy Place — and he assumes taps for drawing it.
27:
Ten stands come next, and the witnesses agree first on what they were for. Gill calls them seats or settles for the lavers described afterwards; Clarke calls them pedestals for the same; Delitzsch explains that the name is taken from their office, to support the basins in which the flesh of the sacrifices was washed. He gives them as square chests cast in brass, four cubits each way and three high.

The construction occupies Delitzsch closely. The sides were flat panels set between frames that enclosed them and were joined at the angles, and within those frames stood figures of lions, oxen and cherubim. He rejects the report that each side was divided into three compartments, both because the text does not say so and because such a division would have left the figures absurdly small. Above the frames he places a pedestal for the basin, resting on the chest, and defends reading the word as a noun rather than an adverb, since taking it adverbially yields no suitable sense. Gill treats the figures as ornament, and notes that since the cherubim are distinguished from the lions and the oxen they must have been figures of something else — of men, or, as Josephus took it, of eagles.

Then the wheels, and here the witnesses divide over a plain question: were the stands meant to move? Delitzsch says they were. The chests rested not directly on the axles but on four feet fixed to them, which lifted each chest clear of the wheel rims so that the ornamented sides stayed visible; the wheels themselves he compares to ordinary carriage wheels, and he takes the whole arrangement as built so the stands could be driven or easily shifted from place to place. Henry reads it the same way, taking the wheels as provision for removing the lavers as occasion required.

Gill denies it. The plates of brass he understands as flat pieces on which the wheels stood, so that they did not rest on the bare floor, and he concludes that the wheels served only as supports. His reasons are two. They were not set like chariot wheels, in pairs on either side of a carriage, but one at each corner of the square; and once the lavers were put upon them the stands were fixed in a settled place. The disagreement is not about the wording but about what the shape of a thing implies — the same four wheels, read by one witness as a means of carriage and by another as feet that happen to turn.
31:
The top of each stand is the hardest passage in the chapter, and Ellicott says so outright: the wording is most obscure, and unintelligible as the English version gives it. Gill describes what he takes to be meant without much hesitation. On the lid of the chest rose a smaller base, circular like a coronet and hollow within, so that the foot of the laver could sit down into it; it went up straight for half a cubit, widened for another half, and stood a cubit high in all, and the circuit of that opening is what the text calls the mouth.

Delitzsch builds the same shape from the other end. The chest was closed above by a dome-like covering, and in the centre of that covering stood a raised piece resembling the capital of a pillar, into which the basin was set by its lower rim; the verse describes that pedestal, and so explains the phrase about what lay beneath the laver. Ellicott quotes this reconstruction at length and will not accept it. To render the same word mouth first of the laver and then of the crown is arbitrary, he objects, and the passage remains dark even after the substitution.

What Ellicott offers instead is tentative and practical. Since the circular stand was half a cubit deep, the underside of the laver looks to have sat a cubit above the mouth; and if the basin were emptied by a tap near its bottom, that circular stand may have been there to catch the drippings. The engraved panels he explains from the geometry: a square top carrying a round stand leaves a space at each corner, and those spaces are probably what the text means.

Below, the description returns to the wheels and their fittings, where the witnesses simply agree. Delitzsch gives four wheels beneath the panels with their axles joined to the chest, each wheel a cubit and a half high, and everything about them — axles, naves, felloes, spokes — cast rather than assembled. Gill matches the wheel to a chariot wheel in form and fashion, and reports the Targum to the same effect; he calls the four supports at the corners pillars, and Delitzsch notes that they were not attached but came out of the base itself. On the arched lid the two are together again. Delitzsch has the upper part of the chest rounded rather than flat, the vaulting standing half a cubit above the sides, with its holders and panels cast out of the same piece; Gill identifies that round compass with the coronet he had already described, rising half a cubit and widening half a cubit more.
36:
The engraving on the stands draws one curiosity from Gill. The word rendered ledges here is not the word used earlier; the Targum takes it for the axle trees, as though the axles and the rims and rings of the wheels were what carried the carving. But the term literally means hands, and Gill reports the tradition preserved by Procopius Gazaeus that the upper part of each stand bore the figures of hands holding a circle like a crown. Delitzsch keeps to what was cut into the metal: cherubim, lions and palm trees, set according to the space each had, with wreaths running round.

The summary that follows is what Delitzsch makes most of. He reads it as insisting on uniformity — one casting, one measure, one form for all ten — and pairs the stands with the ten basins, each of forty baths and four cubits. That measure, he argues, can only be the width, since the basins sat on top of the stands rather than inside them, and one basin belonged to each stand. From this he infers their profile: four cubits across the top against a crown of only a cubit and a half to receive them, which gives a vessel shaped like a wide-spreading shell. Gill lets the verse stand as a summary of what he has already described.

On the lavers themselves the witnesses turn from measurement to use. Gill recalls that the tabernacle had a single laver, and that nobody knows what became of it — some Jewish writers place it in this temple with the ten ranged five on either side of it. The ten were for washing what was to be burnt, and Gill takes them as a figure of the provision made in the blood of Christ, since a believer's works and services and sacrifices, and his person and clothing too, need continual washing there. Clarke divides the labour more exactly: the lavers held water for washing the victims, while the sea was where the priests washed themselves. He steps back a moment to call the whole a work of vast art, labour and expense. Henry gives the capacity in his own terms — about ten barrels apiece — and draws the lesson Gill draws, that those must be very clean who carry the vessels of the Lord, and that the washing is often because the defilement is daily.

Where everything stood is the last question, and the one place the witnesses hesitate. Delitzsch is firm: right means south and left north, so the stands were ranged along the sides of the hall rather than flanking the altar, and the sea stood forward of them between hall and altar, south-east of the one and south-west of the other. Ellicott agrees on the sea's corner and on the lavers being five to a side. Gill takes the right for the south as commonly understood, then notices the difficulty: the entrance faced east, so a man walking in would have the north on his right hand and the south on his left. He leaves the question where the text leaves it, and Henry is content to say only that the ten ordinarily stood in two rows, five on one side of the court and five on the other.
40:
With the smaller vessels Hiram's work is finished, and the chapter pauses to list what has been made. Delitzsch sets out the shape of the section: the brass of the court first, then a second run through the pillars, the stands and their basins, the sea and the lesser vessels, with notes on the metal and the casting, and after that the gold of the Holy Place. He observes that the list runs almost word for word with the Chronicler's, except that the Chronicler also describes the brazen altar, the golden lampstands, the table of shewbread and the laying out of the great court, none of which is mentioned here.

That silence about the altar troubles Ellicott as well. Some have supposed the old altar David reared was kept in use; but the Chronicler and Josephus both say expressly that Hiram made a brazen altar, and give its size, so Ellicott concludes the omission here is simply a gap in the record rather than evidence of anything. He also corrects the rendering: what this verse calls lavers should be pots, as it is translated a few lines later, and the verse describes Hiram completing his commission with the small work after the great.

Gill has already reached the same conclusion about the word and supports it from Jarchi and Ben Gersom, who identify these lavers with the pots used to carry away the ashes of the altar. He explains the other two in the same practical spirit — the shovels were a kind of besom for sweeping the ashes off, the basins were for catching the blood of the sacrifices and sprinkling it — and he too notices what is missing, both the brazen altar and the fleshhooks for lifting meat out of the pots. Henry lingers on the same utensils and on their number: they made abundance of them, so that when the first wore out there would be a stock to draw on. He reads that as foresight rather than excess, Solomon providing for those who would come after.

Clarke stands back from the list altogether. What astonishes him is the speed: that one artist, however many assistants he had, could design and execute works of this magnitude, taste and variety in so short a time. Against these internal works, he says, the mere building of the house was a small matter.

The repeated inventory gives Delitzsch two textual notes. The phrase that puts the capitals upon the face of the pillars he takes for a slip, since one cannot properly say a capital stands on a pillar's surface; the reading should be upon the two pillars. And he rejects as apocryphal an addition the Greek translators carry here, counting forty-eight pillars for the king's house and the house of God — the very combination of the two houses gives it away, though at least one scholar has defended it as a genuine notice.
46:
The casting was done away from the city, and the witnesses explain why. Henry says the ground in the valley was stiff and clayey, fit for making the moulds, and adds a second reason: Solomon would not have dirty, smoky work of this kind carried on in or near Jerusalem. Gill describes the process — the clay being thick and close, moulds were formed in the ground and the melted brass poured into them to take its shape — and notes that although the text credits the king with the casting, the work was Hiram's, done at his orders. Clarke agrees that the particular clay was what drew them there, and reports that opinion is divided over which bank of the river the foundry stood on, one writer placing it near Bethshan.

Delitzsch settles the geography with some care. Succoth lay beyond the Jordan, on the south side of the Jabbok rather than at the ford near Bethshan; Zarthan lay on this side, probably at the height now called Kurn Sartabeh. The casting-place itself must have been on the western side, since the eastern bank has almost no level ground; and he cites a traveller's report that the soil there is marly throughout, which is what the phrase about thickened earth describes — the forms stamped into the clay of the ground. Ellicott gives the same two places with their tribal territories and recalls what happened at each, Jacob's halt on the way home and Gideon's quarrel with the townsmen. One curiosity separates the witnesses here: Gill reads the site as the plain of Jericho where the others read the plain of Jordan.

The weighing is the last note, and it is a negative one. Gill says the vessels were brought from the place of casting and laid up in the sanctuary without being weighed, because they were so many and some of them so large; the Targum reads the verb as laying them up. Delitzsch will not allow that sense — the king let them lie unweighed, as the following clause about the weight of the brass never being ascertained makes plain. He adds where the metal came from: David had taken it from the cities of Hadadezer, with more presented by Toi.

Ellicott names those cities and wonders aloud how they came to be so rich in brass, pointing to the very old copper workings in the Sinai peninsula and to the striking passage on mining in the book of Job. Henry finds the omission creditable on both sides — the workmen were honest enough that no account was needed, and the supply plentiful enough that none was feared short. The quantity, he insists, should be credited to Solomon's care in providing so much, not to carelessness in failing to keep the tally.
48:
The gold comes last, and Henry notes that the work of the house ended with it. Everything within doors was gold and everything was new — except the ark with its mercy-seat and cherubim — the old furniture being melted down or laid aside. Gill says the same of the inventory: all that had stood in the tabernacle was made again, those three pieces excepted. Delitzsch sorts the list by its materials, finding two classes of vessels made of costly gold and a third, named last, of gold less pure, and he warns against narrowing the phrase about the house of the Lord to the Holy Place alone, since here as earlier it covers the temple with its courts.

Ellicott takes the golden altar as the altar of incense and explains what stood behind its use. Incense was burnt on it morning and evening; its horns were touched with the blood of the sin offering, and it was purified with sacrificial blood on the Day of Atonement. The offering of incense therefore presupposed a sacrifice already made, and symbolised worship offered by a man restored to communion with God — the priest entering alone while the people stood praying outside. Ellicott reads it forward to the intercession of the one Mediator. On the loaves he presses the Hebrew, bread of the face or presence, which the Greek rendered bread of offering: a gift returned to God out of what God had given, a kind of first-fruits acknowledging that the whole sustenance of life comes from him.

The number of the lampstands interests three of the witnesses. Gill sets them in the Holy Place before the oracle, ten of them as there were ten tables, and reports the Jewish tradition that ranged them on either side of the old lampstand of Moses rather than of the room; he takes the multiplication as a figure of the greater light the gospel gives. Henry reads the ten tables and ten lampstands the same way, as greater plenty of spiritual food and of heavenly light than the law afforded, and supposes the one table named here was the largest, the rest standing to it as side-boards. Ellicott weighs whether the ten replaced the old sevenfold lampstand or stood beside it, and prefers the second: it is unlikely the ancient vessel was set aside, and the second temple had only the one, which the Arch of Titus shows being carried in the Roman triumph. He notes that Josephus, in full rhetorical flight, claims ten thousand of each, though even he distinguishes the proper lampstand and table from the rest.

The smaller implements draw Ellicott into the vocabulary. The flowers, lamps and tongs are the parts of the lampstand — ornament, light and trimming-tool. The word rendered snuffers comes from a root meaning to prune and is used elsewhere of pruning knives, which is why some translate knives. The spoons are named from a word meaning simply something hollow, and were probably pans for incense; and the rendering censers he judges plainly wrong, since the vessels are snuff-dishes or ash-pans. Gill adds the plainest of these notes, that the bowls were to keep the oil in.

Even the door fittings were gold. Delitzsch thinks these may be of the inferior sort, and takes them for the sockets in which the door pegs turned rather than hinges proper, fitted to the doors of the Holy Place and the Most Holy. Henry seizes on the detail — that everything might be alike magnificent, and Solomon's generosity show in the smallest part of it. He passes on the suggestion that the splendour was meant to keep the people from idolatry, no idol-temple being so rich, and answers it in one line: how little the expedient availed, the event showed.
51:
The chapter ends twice over: the work is finished, and then something older is carried in. Gill takes the first clause as covering everything Solomon ordered made and put into the house, whether for its ornament or for its use and service, and notes that the whole was completed within seven years.

The second clause raises a question Clarke thinks the verse itself answers. Did Solomon spend any of the silver and gold his father had laid up? Apparently not: only after the house stood finished, with all its profusion of gold already in place, are David's dedicated things brought in. Clarke draws the inference that the four years before building began were spent in preparation, and that the king went on appropriating part of the public revenue throughout the work, so that what his father had gathered could simply be stored. The temple was therefore truly Solomon's, he concludes — he found the materials and bore every expense — while what David gave went into the treasury untouched. Clarke adds that the whole was built in some measure on the model of the older tent and dedicated to the same use, and sends his reader back to that earlier description for the pattern.

Ellicott is interested in the size and the spirit of what David had gathered. The accumulation was enormous, and evidently the work of years, drawn out of the spoils of many victories; he points to the words in which David himself offered it, that both riches and honour come from God, and that what was given had first been received from him. Ellicott also reads the wording closely enough to notice that more than vessels came in: besides the gold, silver and brass already worked, there was bullion in money or in ingots laid up in the sacred treasury.

Henry asks what the reserve was for and answers practically — whatever the building and furnishing had not consumed went into the treasury against repairs, emergencies and the standing charge of the temple service. Then he turns it toward the reader. What parents have dedicated to God, children ought by no means to take back or divert; the right course is to devote it cheerfully to the uses it was meant for, and Henry attaches the promise that those who do will inherit the blessing along with the estate.
